We assessed depressive symptoms using the 20-item Centre for Epidemiologic Studies for Depression Scale (CES-D), and measured dietary diversity as the number of five food groups consumed in previous 24-hours. We used linear regression to estimate the association between high dietary diversity (consumption of all the five food groups) and continuous depression scores, adjusting for covariate sets. We tested for effect modification by wealth status, and ran quantile regression to explore variation across depression scores distributions. Results: Higher dietary diversity was associated with fewer depressive symptoms [adjusted β (95% CI): -3.19 (-6.40, 0.02)], with stronger effect among individuals with low wealth [adjusted β (95% CI): -6.12 (-10.71, -1.52)] relative to those with higher wealth [adjusted β (95% CI): -0.06 (-4.31, 4.25); Wald p-value interaction =0.05]. Effect sizes were larger at higher quantiles, notably at 50th [adjusted β (95% CI): -4.20(-8.65, 0.25)], 75th [adjusted β (95% CI): -2.62 (-8.56, 3.36)] and 90th [adjusted β (95% CI): -3.2 (-10.06, 3.66)] quantiles. Conclusion: In rural western Kenya, higher dietary diversity was associated with lower depression scores, particularly among low-wealth individuals, and those with severe symptoms. Findings suggest that improving dietary diversity may offer mental health benefit for socioeconomically disadvantaged individuals in resource poor settings. Future work could leverage longitudinal and experimental studies for improved inference.
score_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of dietary diversity and depression; no advanced methods.

title: Exploring Maternal-Fetal Stress Dynamics: A Feasibility Analysis
abstract: Background: Stress-induced pregnancy complications are significant contributors to preterm labor and maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Chronic psychosocial stress has been linked to biophysiological damage, including accelerated telomere shortening in women and their offspring. These stressors are particularly impactful for pregnant women living in high-stress environments, where various psychosocial factors complicate the ability to carry a healthy pregnancy. Objectives: This study aims to assess the adverse health effects of repeated stress on pregnant women and capture their journey, especially those from high-stress environments, as they seek and receive prenatal care. Methods: This study recruited 35 female adults aged 21 and older who were between 27 and 39 weeks of gestation from healthcare centers. The participants were exposed to a slightly stressful video, a humorous video, and a relaxing video and response to stressors was assessed using the Tobii Pro Nano, the Shimmer, and salivary cortisol. Visual and numerical data were exported from Tobii Pro Lab and were analyzed using SPSS V. 27. Multivariate analyses, including t-tests, were used to evaluate the study aims. Results: Preliminary findings indicate the feasibility of conducting a larger-scale investigation into the impact of chronic stress on pregnancy outcomes. Analysis revealed key barriers and facilitators affecting access to prenatal care and maternal autonomy in implementing stress management strategies during gestation. These findings will inform the design of targeted interventions aimed at reducing stress and improving maternal-fetal health outcomes. Physiological data provide evidence of psychosocial stress effects, with fetal heart rate changes demonstrating a significant positive correlation with maternal heart rate (r = 0.64, p < 0.05) and exhibiting simultaneous stabilization patterns, suggesting a dynamic maternal-fetal stress response linkage. Conclusion: This feasibility study represents a critical step in understanding and addressing the complex interplay between psychosocial stress and pregnancy outcomes in different communities.
score_reason: Feasibility analysis in maternal stress; weak methodological content.

title: State-Level Geographic Hotspots and Temporal Pattern of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Virus Occurrence in Turkey Across the United States, 2022-2025
abstract: The U.S. turkey industry faces challenges from the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAI) H5N1, leading to economic losses caused by turkey deaths and trade restrictions. However, little research has examined geographic hotspots and temporal patterns of HPAI H5N1 in turkeys across the U.S., despite their important role in guiding targeted strategies for these areas. This study aimed to investigate geographic hotspots and temporal patterns of HPAI H5N1 in turkeys at the U.S. state level. We retrieved data on HPAI H5N1 in turkeys from February 2022 to September 2025 from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) surveillance. Global Moran’s index (I) statistics were computed to detect global spatial autocorrelation. The geographic hotspots of HPAI H5N1 occurrence were investigated using Kulldorff’s circular scan statistics (CSSS). Between February 2022 and September, 484 events of HPAI H5N1 were recorded in turkeys across U.S. states, with an observed concentration of HPAI H5N1 detections in the upper Midwest states: Minnesota (n = 137) and South Dakota (n = 110). Detection of HPAI H5N1 varied by season, with the highest occurrence in winter (33%;158/484), followed by fall (32%; 156/484), spring (31%; 149/484), and summer (4%; 21/484). Global Moran’s test showed significant positive spatial autocorrelation in the occurrence of HPAI H5N1 in turkeys at the state level (I = 0.25, p = 0.020). A primary geographic hotspot was identified using CSSS, encompassing Minnesota, South Dakota, Iowa, and Wisconsin (RR = 16.4; p < 0.0001). This study identifies geographic hotspots for HPAI H5N1 detections in the upper Midwest states, revealing an increase in detections during the cooler months, while minimal detections occurred during the summer. These findings can guide targeted strategies in hotspot areas, such as educating turkey farmers on HPAI H5N1 transmission and biosecurity measures.
score_reason: Spatial-temporal analysis of HPAI; applied, no statistical novelty.

title: Metabolic syndrome and memory decline: evidence from a longitudinal aging cohort in rural South Africa
abstract: Introduction: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with increased risk of dementia in high-income countries. Given the different etiologic processes and population conditions driving MetS prevalence, it is unclear if MetS and dementia will show similar associations in low- and middle-income settings. Methods: Mixed effects linear regression models were used to estimate the association between dichotomous MetS status and memory decline for individuals in the South African HAALSA Indepth cohort and by age and sex strata. An interaction term between MetS and time allowed the slope to vary by MetS status. Results: MetS was associated with higher baseline memory scores (β = 0.07 SD units, 95% CI = 0.02, 0.13) and faster memory decline over time (β = -0.01 SD units/year, 95% CI = -0.02, 0.00). Discussion: Our findings suggest that MetS status could be an important marker for identifying groups at higher risk of dementia in low-resource settings.
score_reason: Longitudinal aging study with mixed effects regression; standard methods, no advanced causal inference.

title: Excess mortality following discharge from substance use disorder treatment in Chile, 2010–2020
abstract: Background: People with a history of substance use disorder treatment (SUT) have excess mortality, but national estimates in Chile are scarce. We quantified mortality after discharge from publicly funded SUT compared with the general population, and examined variation by sex, age, setting, primary substance, and treatment completion. Methods: We linked the national registry of publicly funded psychosocial treatment episodes (2010–2020) to the national mortality registry to form a retrospective cohort of adults aged 18–64. Follow-up began at first episode termination and ended at death or December 31, 2020. Outcomes were all-cause and ICD-10 cause-specific deaths. We estimated age-, sex-, and year-adjusted directly standardized rates per 1,000 person-years (PY) and the standardized mortality ratio (SMR) with 95% CI overall and by subgroups. Results: Among 70,064 patients (24% women; median age 35), 2,996 deaths occurred over 353,826 person-years (adjusted rate 13.1 per 1,000 PY). Overall SMR was 3.5 (95% CI 3.3–3.8). Relative risk was higher in women (SMR=5.5 vs. men 3.3), patients whose primary substance was alcohol (4.7 vs. illicit 2.7), those treated in residential programs (4.8 vs. ambulatory 3.4), and with incomplete treatments (3.9 vs. completed 2.8). Excess risk was pronounced soon after discharge and peaked in mid-adulthood (Figure 1). External-cause mortality was elevated, including intentional self-harm (SMR=4.9), unintentional injuries (3.9), and assault (3.6). Non-external excess was greatest for digestive (6.2), respiratory (4.1), and infectious diseases (3.0). Conclusions: Adults in Chile with a history of publicly funded SUT experienced about 3.5-fold higher mortality than expected, driven by self-harm, injuries, assault, and digestive and respiratory conditions. Women and people treated for alcohol use faced the highest relative risk. Findings support strengthening treatment retention, integrated mental health care, and sustained post-discharge surveillance.
score_reason: Retrospective cohort study using registry data; standard survival analysis.

title: Body size and composition in relation to the risk of thyroid autoimmunity in children: A prospective analysis in the TEDDY cohort
abstract: Childhood growth has been shown to correlate with islet autoantibody development in type 1 diabetes, however, the role of growth in other organ-specific autoimmunity remains unclear. We aimed to longitudinally assess the relationships of body size and composition with risk of thyroid autoimmunity in children. The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young (TEDDY) is a prospective cohort in the US and Europe following children at increased genetic risk for several autoimmune diseases, including thyroid autoimmunity. Children were followed from birth to age 15 years with visits occurring 2 – 4 times per year. They were screened for thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin autoantibodies as a measure of thyroid autoimmunity near ages 9 and 14 years, and children autoantibody positive were retrospectively tested in previously collected samples. Height and weight were measured at every study visit, while body composition was measured at every study visit starting from early adolescence. Bayesian joint models were used to examine relationships between the risk for thyroid autoimmunity and either height z-score, weight z-score, BMI z-score, body fat %, fat mass (kg), or lean mass (kg). Among 5188 children screened, 542 had thyroid autoimmunity. Height was the only growth metric associated with risk of thyroid autoimmunity (HR per SD 1.13 95% CrI 1.04, 1.24). The association was strongest between ages 3 – 8 years (Figure 1). While the interaction with sex was not significant, the estimate was higher in girls than in boys (HR 1.21 95% CrI 1.09, 1.36; HR 0.99 95% CrI 0.84, 1.17, respectively). Mid-parental target height was also positively associated with risk of thyroid autoimmunity (HR 1.02 per cm, 95% CI 1.003, 1.035). A child’s height was associated with an increased risk of thyroid autoimmunity. Understanding the mechanisms that link height to autoimmunity is essential to uncover the biological pathways that may influence childhood autoimmune thyroid disease.
score_reason: Prospective cohort analysis of body size and autoimmunity; simple longitudinal regression.

title: A simulation of potential air cleaning interventions to reduce Long COVID incidence and disease burden
abstract: Over five years after the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, widespread transmission of the SARS-COV-2 virus has left millions with Long COVID, a multisystem disorder characterized by ongoing and sometimes disabling symptoms that persist after an acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. Importantly, Long COVID can develop not only after an individual’s first SARS-CoV-2 infection but also after a reinfection, even if they recovered successfully from prior infection(s). Population-level surveys in the US find that more than 5% of the population currently experiences Long COVID, and the natural recovery rate of Long COVID is currently estimated to be less than 5%. Given this substantial disease burden, strategies to reduce Long COVID incidence and prevalence are urgently needed. We constructed a cohort-state transition model to estimate the reduction in disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) associated with a range of evidence-based non-pharmaceutical interventions, including installation of HEPA filtration and far-germicidal UV disinfection in public spaces and returns to masking in healthcare and other public settings. Preliminary estimates reveal that widespread adoption of HEPA filtration and far-germicidal UV disinfection has the potential to reduce Long COVID-associated DALYs by 127 DALYs per 1000 persons over a 10-year period. These interventions hold substantial promise for reducing the ongoing risk of Long COVID by reducing the spread of SARS-COV-2 in public spaces.
score_reason: Simulation study of air cleaning interventions, basic modeling, no causal inference methodology.

title: The Role of Parent-Paediatrician Relationship on Preventive Medical Care Utilization among U.S. children aged 1-17: Results from the National Survey of Children’s Health 2022-2023
abstract: Introduction: The relationship between the parent and their child’s pediatrician is crucial for optimal preventive medical care utilization. The study aims to determine how the quality of the relationship affects the use of preventive health care services among children in the US. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis using data from the 2022-2023 National Survey of Children’s Health, focusing on U.S. children aged 1–17. Descriptive statistics and logistic regression were conducted to examine the associations and internal consistency of the parent-pediatrician relationship index. Results: Of 109,246 children, 23.7% (31,304) had a high parent-pediatrician relationship. Children from households with a high parent-pediatrician relationship demonstrated increased odds of utilizing preventive medical care (aOR=7.87,95% CI:7.00–8.85). Household incomes ≥400% FPL (aOR=1.31,95% CI: 1.15–1.50), parents with some college education (aOR=1.34,95% CI: 1.14–1.59), or a college degree (aOR=2.05,95% CI:1.73–2.42), and children in households of four had significantly higher odds of preventive care utilization (aOR=1.22,95%CI: 1.06–1.41). On the contrary, compared to children aged 1-3, children aged 4–7 (aOR=0.65,95%CI: 0.58–0.74), 8–11 (aO=0.41,95% CI: 0.36–0.46), 11–14 (aOR=0.33,95% CI: 0.29–0.38), and 15–17 (aOR=0.29,95% CI: 0.26–0.33) had significantly lower odds of preventive care utilization. Compared to uninsured children, the odds of utilizing preventive medical care for children with public insurance and private insurance only were (aOR 4.08, 95% CI: 3.52-4.74) and (aOR 3.14, 95% CI: 2.71-3.63), respectively. Conclusions: The findings of this study suggest that strengthening the parent-pediatrician relationship plays a critical role in the utilization of preventive care among children, highlighting the need for personalized healthcare strategies.
score_reason: Cross-sectional logistic regression, standard epidemiological methods without advanced statistics.

title: Trends in Place-based Disparities in Cancer Risk Factors and Cancer Screening Utilization in the U.S., 1997-2023
abstract: Background: We examined trends in urban-rural disparities in cancer risk factors and cancer screening utilization among U.S. counties from 1997 to 2023. Methods: This was a county-level ecological study. Prevalences of four cancer risk factors (tobacco use, excessive drinking, obesity, physical inactivity) among adults aged ≥18 in 2011 -2022 were obtained from the County Health Ranking & Roadmaps. Prevalences of guideline recommended cancer screening (mammography and Pap Smear) in 1997-2023 were extracted from the National Cancer Institute’s Small Area Estimates. Counties’ metropolitan status was determined by 2013 Rural-Urban Continuum Codes. Prevalence ratio (PR, urban vs. rural) of each outcome was calculated for each year. P-trend was calculated to capture the changes in PR over time. Results: Among 3,143 counties, the prevalence of obesity, excessive drinking, and mammography use increased while the prevalence of tobacco use, physical inactivity, and Pap Smear use decreased over the study period (Figure 1). Urban-rural disparities widened for tobacco use (PR increased from 1.06 to 1.16, P-trend=0.0013) and obesity (PR increased from 1.04 to 1.06, P-trend=0.027). For excessive drinking, rural residents initially had lower prevalence but experienced faster increases over time, resulting in similar prevalence levels between urban and rural areas in recent years. Disparities in physical inactivity also widened, although changes were not statistically significant. For cancer screening, disparities in mammography use narrowed (PR decreased from 1.11 to 1.02, P-trend=0.02), whereas disparities in Pap Smear use remained unchanged. Conclusion: County-level urban-rural disparities have widened over the past decades for several cancer risk factors, including tobacco use, obesity, and physical inactivity. Community-level interventions and policies that promote healthy lifestyles are needed to reduce place-based disparities in cancer risk and prevention.
score_reason: Ecological trend analysis, descriptive epidemiology, no relevant statistical methodology.

title: Log-binomial modeling of association between risky driving behaviours and incident road traffic crashes during the past one-year among young adults in a middle eastern country
abstract: Objective: This cross-sectional study assessed the one-year period prevalence of road traffic crashes (RTCs) among adults in Kuwait, the frequency of hand-held mobile phone use while driving, and examined the association between hand-held cell phone use and RTC status during the past-one year. Methods: During December 2021, a cross-sectional study was conducted using a self-administered e-questionnaire through social media platforms among adult driver residents of Kuwait aged ≥ 18 years, of either gender, or any nationality. We computed the one-year period-prevalence of RTC (one or more vs. none) and the frequency of hand-held cell phone use while driving (irregular vs. regular). Multivariable log-binomial regression analysis was carried out to identify the variables significantly (p <0.05) and independently associated with RTC status. Adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR) and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used to interpret the final model. Results: Of 1755 participants, 696 (39.7%) were 18-25 years old, 1022 (58.2%) females, and 1551 (88.4%) were Kuwaiti. Of the participants, 85.2% (1496/1755) regularly used mobile phone while driving during the past-year. The one-year period prevalence of RTC was 26% (456/1755). Multivariable log-binomial regression model showed that the participants were significantly more likely to have had encountered one or more RCTs during the past one year, if they were regular user of mobile phone while driving (aPR = 1.88; 95% CI: 1.32 – 2.68; p = 0.001) or have had a tendency to disregard the traffic rules while driving (aPR = 1.22; 95% CI: 1.02 –1.47; p = 0.031). Moreover, compared with the participants who always respected the speed limit law, the participants who tended to disdain the speed limit law were significantly more likely to have experienced one or more RTC during the past one-year (aPR = 1.35; 95% CI: 1.12 – 1.62; p = 0.002). Furthermore, compared with the participants having driving experience of less than 1 year, the participants tended to have one more RTC during the past one year if they have had 1-3 years (aPR = 1.77; 95% CI = 1.22 – 2.58, p = 0.003) or 4-6 years (aPR = 1.61; 95% CI: 1.10 – 2.35; p = 0.014) of driving experience. Additionally, compared with the participants aged 36-years old or older, participants were significantly more likely to have encountered one or more RCT during the past one year, if they were in the age band of 26-35 years (aPR = 1.52; 95% CI: 1.19 – 1.95; p = 0.001) or 18-25 years (aPR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.21 – 2.30; p = 0.002). Conclusion: The study showed a high one-year period prevalence of RTC, and high frequency of regular mobile phone use while driving. The risky driving behaviours that were significantly associated with RTC status during the past one-year included younger age, regular hand-held mobile phone use while driving, driving experience and regular violation of speed limit. Focused educational intervention may alleviate RTC burden in this and other similar settings. If implemented, future studies may look at the effect of such an intervention.
score_reason: Cross-sectional log-binomial modeling, standard epidemiological regression, no advanced methodology.

title: The Association of the Supply of OBGYNs with Abortion Access in the United States
abstract: Background & Objective: On June 24, 2022, the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health decision overturned Roe v. Wade, shifting decision-making about abortion access to the states. There has been substantial media coverage surrounding fears that changes in legal access may drive physicians from abortion restrictive states. We sought to explore the association between state-level abortion access and the supply of OBGYNs and determine if there is any evidence of shifting trends based on abortion law exposure. Methods: We regressed state-level physician counts from 2018 and 2023, obtained from the American Medical Association and made available by the American Association of Medical Colleges, against a constructed binary indicator of abortion access to assess the association between abortion law and supply of each group of physicians before and after changes in the law. Models were adjusted for population. An alternative exposure metric including abortion law and anti-LGBTQ policies was used in sensitivity analysis. Results: 25 states are categorized as abortion restrictive; 25 states plus DC are protective of abortion rights. States restricting abortion access after Dobbs were found to have significantly lower rates of OBGYNs in comparison with protective states, with no evidence to indicate shifts in supply after Dobbs as of the end of 2023. (OBGYN 2018 Rate Ratio (RR): 0.72, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.65, 0.80, p<0.001; OBGYN 2023 RR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.64, 0.78.) Using the constructed exposure metric, higher degrees of autonomy restrictions are associated with fewer OBGYNs, demonstrating evidence of a linear trend. Conclusion: We found fewer OBGYNs practicing in states that moved to restrict abortion access after Dobbs both before and after the decision, with no evidence of changes in the overall supply nationwide as of the end of 2023. Lower rates of physicians in restrictive states may be a predictor of decreased access to care for populations in those states. Physician supply information should be followed to track any changes occurring, particularly given the lag present in available data.
score_reason: Simple regression of state-level data; limited statistical complexity.

title: Epidemiological impacts of urban noise pollution on oral health in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Urban noise pollution is a growing environmental exposure in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet its links to oral health remain poorly understood. Chronic noise exposure contributes to physiologic stress, sleep disturbance, cardiovascular dysregulation, and altered cortisol patterns—mechanisms that may influence periodontal disease, bruxism, salivary dysfunction, and oral pain. This scoping review mapped the existing evidence on noise pollution as a determinant of oral-health outcomes in LMICs and identified gaps to guide future epidemiologic research. We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and regional databases for studies assessing environmental noise and any oral-health indicator, including periodontal status, caries prevalence, bruxism, temporomandibular disorders, salivary biomarkers, or oral-health–related quality of life. Eligible study designs included observational epidemiologic studies, exposure-assessment reports, and physiologic investigations linking noise to oral stress-response pathways. Two reviewers independently screened articles and charted data on exposure measures, oral outcomes, analytic approaches, and LMIC context. Fourteen studies met inclusion criteria, most conducted in rapidly urbanizing regions of South Asia, Latin America, and West Africa. Noise exposure was typically assessed using environmental decibel mapping or self-reported residential noise burden. Across studies, higher noise exposure was associated with increased prevalence of bruxism, elevated salivary cortisol, greater periodontal inflammation, and higher reports of orofacial pain, though heterogeneity in exposure measurement limited comparability. No longitudinal or population-representative studies were identified, and no studies used objective personal noise monitoring. This review demonstrates emerging evidence linking urban noise pollution to adverse oral-health outcomes in LMICs but highlights significant methodological gaps. Standardized exposure metrics, longitudinal designs, and integration of physiologic stress biomarkers are needed to advance causal inference and inform environmental-health policy.
score_reason: Scoping review on noise pollution and oral health; not a primary data analysis.
key_techniques: environmental noise exposure assessment (dB mapping, self-report)

title: Mapping Food Is Medicine Across Texas: Regional and Demographic Disparities in Program Availability
abstract: Objective: To assess the geographic and demographic distribution of Food Is Medicine (FIM) programs in Texas and identify disparities relative to diet-related chronic disease burden. Methods: We conducted a statewide landscape scan (Dec 2024–Apr 2025) using a questionnaire distributed to FIM implementers. Program data were integrated with county-level chronic disease prevalence from CDC PLACES and visualized using GIS mapping to evaluate FIM availability and disease burden. Results: The analysis revealed 48 unique FIM programs across Texas and significant geographical and population-level disparities in their distribution, with programs available in only 62 of 254 Texas counties, leaving 76% of counties without any FIM presence. Programs were concentrated in urban areas: Harris County (27 programs: 16 Medically Tailored Groceries (MTG), 5 Produce Prescription (PRx), 2 Medically Tailored Meals (MTM), 2 Culinary Medicine) and Fort Bend (8 programs). MTG accounted for 54% of all programs, while PRx and MTM represented 17% and 10%, respectively. Counties with the highest age-adjusted diet-related chronic disease prevalence, including diabetes (21–24%), hypertension (36–39%), and obesity (45–50%), had no FIM programs. Disparities were also observed in 28% of programs serving pregnant, pre-, and postpartum women, highlighting demographic gaps. Conclusion: FIM programs in Texas are unevenly distributed, leaving high-need rural and underserved communities without access to nutrition-based interventions. These findings provide critical evidence to guide policy for equitable scaling of FIM resources to address social determinants of health and reduce chronic disease burden.
score_reason: Descriptive GIS mapping study; no causal or advanced statistical methodology.

title: Understanding Treatment Adherence Barriers and Facilitators in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes: A Mixed-Methods Protocol
abstract: Background: Up to 70% of youth with pediatric type 2 diabetes (T2D) do not fully adhere to their treatment regimen, which includes medication, nutrition, and physical activity. Addressing this gap requires a thorough understanding of personal and sociocultural factors shaping youth and family experiences. Yet, research in this area remains limited, and no evidence-based adherence interventions currently exist for this population. Objective: This mixed-methods study protocol aims to (1) identify daily barriers and facilitators to treatment regimen adherence among youth with T2D and (2) explore youth and parent preferences for culturally appropriate and feasible adherence-promoting intervention strategies. Methods: In Phase 1, youth aged 10–21 years with T2D and their parents were recruited from a pediatric diabetes clinic in Minneapolis. Both parent and child completed a baseline survey on family functioning, mental health, and sociodemographic characteristics. Youth then completed 14 days of ecological momentary assessments (EMA) while wearing an accelerometer and using an electronic pill cap to capture real-time behaviors related to their diet, physical activity, and medication use. In Phase 2, youth and parents participated in qualitative interviews to discuss and expand on EMA findings and identify needs and preferences for future community interventions. Results: Data collection concluded in August 2025. A total of 26 youth aged 10 to 17 completed Phase 1 and 12 completed Phase 2, while 7 young adults aged 18 to 21 completed Phase 1 and 2 of them also completed Phase 2. Conclusions: This protocol was feasible and effective in integrating real-time behavioral data, objective gold-standard measurements, and qualitative insights among youth with T2D. Together, these data provide an in-depth understanding of pediatric T2D treatment regimen adherence barriers and facilitators and will guide the development of culturally responsive, family-centered interventions.
score_reason: Mixed-methods protocol, no data or statistical methodology relevant to primary interests.

title: Mapping the Opportunities: Using Network Analysis to identify Possibilities for engaging Neighborhood Coffee Shops and Diners for Health Promotion in the Community
abstract: Health clinics in the community are the most common sources of health information for the public. Whilst neighborhood barbershops and hair salons have been engaged for health education, ubiquitous coffee shops and diners have yet to be harnessed for health promotion. This study aims to compare community patronage patterns of neighborhood eateries with health clinics and beauty shops, to identify opportunities for health promotion. We conducted a sequential mixed-methods study among residents aged ≥21years from two neighborhoods in Singapore, July 2023-October 2024 (qualitative interviews) and November 2024-April 2025 (questionnaire survey). The community interviews informed the most notable health clinics, eateries, and beauty shops. Visits to these notable shops, along with demographic data, were collected anonymously via an online survey distributed to all households in the neighborhoods. Using a two-mode network linking survey respondents and shops they visited in the past 12 months, we identified shops with the highest degrees of centrality, representing those most frequently visited. Interviews with 60 residents achieved data saturation on the 62 most notable shops. Of 403 respondents of the online survey, 365 have visited at least one of the shops in the preceding 12 months. Among the patrons, the mean age was 50.3 (SD 14.8) years, 54.5% were female and 87.1% were Chinese. Eateries had the highest degrees of centrality (median 47, max 98), followed by clinics (median 18, max 71) and beauty shops (median 5, max 18). The reach of the top three highest degree-of-centrality eateries included residents of both gender and all ethnic and age groups (21-34, 35-49, 50 years and above). Neighborhood coffee shops and diners have higher community patronage than health clinics and beauty shops. They are also visited by all segments of the population. Neighborhood eateries could be leveraged to expand the reach of health education and promotion efforts in the community.
score_reason: Mixed-methods community study, network analysis but not statistical network models, low relevance.

title: Mind the Gap: Addressing Missing Person Time When Estimating Outcome Incidence in Longitudinal Data
abstract: Background: Longitudinal data often include gaps in observation when outcomes (and other variables) are unmeasured due to missed study visits or dropout. We explore the fundamentals of data gaps and use simulation to compare approaches for handling data gaps when estimating outcome incidence. Methods: We generated a simulation of 1000 individuals across 10 study visits. We used 4 data-generating mechanisms: (1) missingness was independent of the outcome; (2) there was a baseline common cause of missingness and the outcome; (3) there was a time-varying common cause; and (4) the outcome directly affected future missingness. We estimated the risk and rate of the first outcome occurrence (generated as a transient, repeated, and permanent outcome), using crude and adjusted approaches, across 1000 iterations, and compared bias and empirical standard error. Results: Under Scenario 1, in crude analyses, results were unbiased when censoring before a data gap but not when allowing participants to return. Under scenarios 2–4, all crude approaches were biased. Inverse probability of censoring weights and multiple imputation were relatively unbiased across scenarios and outcome types; multiple imputation was more precise. Inverse probability of observation weights was biased when the outcome was permanent and was less precise than either of the other two approaches. Conclusion: Crude approaches allowing participants to return following a data gap are not recommended because they can be biased even when missingness and the outcome are independent. Instead, one should either censor or handle the data gap using multiple imputation.
score_reason: Addresses missing data in longitudinal studies, directly relevant to causal inference methods.

title: Sibling Comparison Designs to Assess Social Exposures and Empirical Tools to Guide Interpretation: An Illustrative Study of Childhood Income and Subsequent Mental Disorders
abstract: Background: Sibling comparison designs are increasingly used to strengthen causal claims about social exposures and health outcomes, yet methodologic challenges in interpreting their results remain insufficiently addressed. This study develops empirical approaches to help assess whether sibling comparison estimates provide reliable evidence for causal relationships. Methods: We used childhood family income and severe mental disorders in a Danish nationwide cohort (n = 643,623; 403,963 siblings born 1986–1996) as an example. We applied three complementary approaches: negative control analyses using pseudo-siblings (unrelated individuals with similar income differences as real siblings) to isolate exposure variability effects from shared familial confounding effects; assessment of sibling age structure, exposure correlation, and variation patterns to establish whether meaningful contrasts exist between siblings; and critical period assumption evaluation through age-specific income measurement. Results: Family income at age 14 was associated with decreased mental disorder risk in the population-wide analysis [adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) = 0.78; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.76, 0.81] but showed no association using a sibling comparison design (aHR = 1.02; 95% CI: 0.94, 1.11). The pseudo-sibling cohort matched on income also showed substantial attenuation (aHR = 0.93; 95% CI: 0.85, 1.01), while pseudo-siblings not matched on income showed no attenuation. Income associations were similar across childhood measurement ages 0–14 (aHR range = 0.67–0.82). Conclusions: In this example, estimates from the sibling comparison design may reflect limited exposure variability within families and unmet life course model assumptions, rather than or in addition to the removal of shared familial confounding. The empirical approaches we developed help researchers distinguish methodologic factors from genuine null findings, and are available with R code for implementation.
score_reason: Develops interpretation tools for sibling comparison designs, a core causal inference method.

title: Where Do Target Trials Come From? Specifying the Protocol of a Target Trial When Repurposing Data for Causal Inference
abstract: Descriptions of the target trial framework often appear to assume that investigators knew the protocol of the target trial from the start of the investigation. In practical applications, however, the protocol of the target trial is constrained by the observational data that investigators have access to. When using preexisting observational databases, the target trial protocol typically needs to be iteratively developed as investigators learn about the data. Here we examine the process by which investigators adapt their original causal question, operationalized into the protocol of a hypothetical trial (the index trial), to the available data. This adaptive process results in a final causal question, operationalized into the protocol of another hypothetical trial (the target trial), that depends both on the original causal question and on the available data. As a result, prespecification of an emulatable target trial protocol is not generally possible because adaptations are expected after inspecting the data. The adaptive nature of the specification of the target trial protocol raises important questions about the types of data examinations that are permissible to guide the adaptations, the procedures for transparent reporting of each adaptation and its rationale, and the possibility of prespecifying the rules that will govern the investigators’ decisions to adapt the protocol to the data.
score_reason: Examines target trial protocol specification, central to causal inference from observational data.

title: Antibiotics and Preterm Delivery: The Prevalent New-user Cohort Design to Resolve Immortal Time Bias
abstract: Background: Observational studies of the association between antibiotics and preterm delivery report conflicting findings, with some potentially affected by immortal time bias. We assessed the effects of third-trimester antibiotic use on preterm delivery and low birthweight, using a study design that accounts for immortal time bias. Methods: We used the UK’s Clinical Practice Research Datalink to identify pregnant females aged 12–50, over the period 2002 to 2016, reaching 27 weeks of gestation without antibiotic use until that point. We applied the prevalent new-user design, matching each third-trimester antibiotic initiator with a reference nonuser at the same gestational day, using time-conditional propensity scores. The 2 matched groups were compared on the incidence of preterm delivery and low birthweight. The full cohort was also analyzed with antibiotic use considered as time-fixed and time-varying exposures. Results: The cohort included 207,027 pregnancies, with 16,865 initiating antibiotics matched to 16,865 nonusers. The hazard ratio (HR) of preterm delivery with third-trimester antibiotic use was 1.14 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.04, 1.24], compared with nonuse. With time-fixed exposure, subject to immortal time bias, the HR was 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73, 0.83), while with time-varying exposure, the HR was 1.23 (95% CI: 1.16, 1.32). The HR of low birthweight with antibiotic initiation was 1.07 (95% CI: 0.93, 1.25) compared with 0.91 (95% CI: 0.83, 1.00) under the time-fixed approach. Conclusions: Using the prevalent new-user design, which emulates a randomized trial, antibiotic use late in pregnancy was associated with a modestly increased incidence of preterm delivery. Previous inconclusive studies may have resulted from observational methods that introduced, or insufficiently addressed, immortal time bias.
score_reason: Directly applies causal inference methods (prevalent new-user design) to address immortal time bias in epidemiology, strongly related to primary interest in causal inference.

title: Applying the Target Study Conceptual Model to Measure Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Hypertension Treatment Intensification
abstract: Background: This tutorial paper demonstrates the application of a conceptual model to measure racial and ethnic disparities in treatment intensification among adults with hypertension consistent with the Institute of Medicine (IOM) definition. The IOM defines disparity as differences in health care quality that are not due to access-related factors, clinical needs, preferences, and appropriateness of intervention (referred to as allowable covariates). Methods: We used a conceptual model called the Target Study to estimate annual disparities in the probability of treatment intensification between Black and White patients seen at primary care clinics within a large healthcare system in the Mid-Atlantic region from 2018 to 2022, using electronic medical record data. We emulated the specified target study through an appropriate study design and the use of inverse probability weighting to balance allowable covariates while measuring disparities. Results: Unadjusted analyses showed a higher percentage of treatment intensification for Black patients compared with White patients, with annual differences ranging from 2 to 4 percentage points. For example, in 2020, the unadjusted difference was three percentage points (95% confidence interval: 1%, 5%). After adjusting for allowable covariates via the emulated target study, Black patients had consistently lower percentages of treatment intensification by 3–4 percentage points each year. For example, in 2020, the adjusted disparity was −3 percentage points (95% confidence interval: −4%, −1%). Conclusions: The Target Study can implement the IOM definition for measuring disparities in health care. Future research should explore its application across different populations to better understand and address health disparities.
score_reason: Tutorial applying target trial model for disparity analysis; clear causal inference methodology.

title: Differential Reporting of Severe Maternal Morbidity on US Birth Certificate and Claims Data by Race and Ethnicity
abstract: Background: US birth certificates are the only complete, national source of severe maternal morbidity (SMM) data, but state and local studies have identified data quality concerns. The objective of this study was to compare reporting of SMM in birth certificate versus hospital claims data and evaluate differences by patient race/ethnicity. Methods: We compared incidence rates of blood transfusion, hysterectomy, intensive care unit admission, uterine rupture, and third/fourth degree perineal laceration between 2019 deliveries in the United States birth certificate and the Premier Healthcare Database, overall and stratifying by maternal race/ethnicity. We then computed incidence rate ratios (IRRs) computed between datasets, and fit logistic regression models of race/ethnicity on SMM. Results: Comparing 3,467,934 birth certificate deliveries with 3,450,569 Premier deliveries (n = 905,766 preweighting for national representativeness), incidence rates of SMMs were lower in birth certificate compared with Premier data, and these rate differentials varied by maternal race/ethnicity. For example, among non-Hispanic white patients, the incidence rate of blood transfusions in birth certificate data was 50% that of the incidence rate in the Premier claims dataset (IRR: 0.50, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.47, 0.52). Among all other races/ethnicities, the incidence rate of blood transfusions was even lower relative to the claims data (IRR range: 0.29–0.39). Adjusted odds ratios for SMM in non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic patients versus non-Hispanic white patients were closer to the null in birth certificate than Premier data (e.g., compared with non-Hispanic white patients, non-Hispanic Black patients had a 16% higher adjusted odds in the birth certificate [95% CI = 1.10, 1.21] data versus an 84% higher adjusted odds of blood transfusion in Premier data [95% CI = 1.79, 1.89]). Conclusions: Birth certificates report substantially less SMM than claims data, with a greater differential in reporting for non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic patients that may bias birth certificate-based research findings.
score_reason: Investigates differential reporting of maternal morbidity, highlights measurement error issues in causal studies.

title: An Improved Pooled Logistic Regression Implementation
abstract: Background: Pooled logistic regression is a popular tool for survival analyses in epidemiology, but can face computational challenges. Commonly, these challenges are addressed through widening time intervals or using a parametric functional form for time. We propose a third option to reduce the computational burden without constraining the functional form for time. Methods: The proposed algorithm operates by restricting the long data set to rows that correspond to unique event times. However, our approach is only compatible when modeling time most flexibly with disjoint indicators. We compared the standard implementation to the proposed implementation in SAS, R, and Python using a publicly available data set. Results: For the example considered, both implementations provided the same point estimates, but the proposed implementation was between 6 and 68 times faster depending on the software. Conclusions: The proposed implementation can greatly simplify estimation of pooled logistic regression models, which is especially important when relying on the bootstrap for inference.
score_reason: Proposes computational improvement for pooled logistic regression, relevant to statistical computing.
key_techniques: data restriction to unique event times

title: State Minimum Wages and Food Insecurity Among Households Receiving Government Food Assistance
abstract: Background: While the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) aims to reduce food insecurity among low-income households, nearly half of recipients remain food insecure. Increasing state minimum wages could help improve food security, but because SNAP benefits are income-dependent, net effects are unclear. Methods: Using the US Current Population Survey Food Security Supplement (2002–2019), we linked households interviewed in two consecutive Decembers to create a 2-year panel. The primary sample included SNAP recipient households with at least one adult working in year 1. The exposure was the average effective state minimum wage (2019 $) for each state and year. We estimated prevalence differences in food insecurity per $1 increase in minimum wage using a within-household linear fixed-effects model adjusting for time-varying economic confounders and concurrent safety-net policies. We investigated variation in the effect by household and family structure, race and ethnicity, and educational attainment using stratified models. Results: Overall estimates were most compatible with protective effects (prevalence difference per 10,000 households: −298, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −673, 77). The strongest protective estimates were for senior-headed (−1,472, 95% CI: −2,869, −76), Hispanic (−865, 95% CI: −1,638, −92), and some college households (−988, 95% CI: −1,664, −312). Estimates for Indigenous households were imprecise and possibly harmful (900, 95% CI: −736, 2,537). Most other subgroup estimates were near zero. Conclusions: Increased minimum wages may modestly support food security for working SNAP households. As SNAP benefit rules evolve, these findings suggest that minimum-wage policies can complement and reinforce the program’s goals to protect low-income households from food hardship.
score_reason: Applied causal question on minimum wages and food insecurity; relevant to causal inference.

title: Discretizing Continuous Event Time Data
abstract: Although data may capture continuous event times or event times with high resolution (e.g., day), some statistical analyses require the discretization of time into intervals and assigning each event (i.e., outcome or loss to follow-up [LTFU]) to the start or end of an interval. First, using a simulated example, we showed that outcomes should be assigned to the end of the interval. Next, we considered four approaches for assigning LTFU events in a simulated example and in 20 real datasets. Comparing the resulting cumulative risk curves with the curve using continuous time, one approach always had the least error: assigning LTFU to the start or end of the interval, depending on which was closest to the continuous event time. This approach was superior to always censoring at the beginning or end of the interval.
score_reason: Methodological guidance on discretization of event times; touches statistical computing.

title: Understanding Algorithmic Fairness for Clinical Prediction in Terms of Subgroup Net Benefit and Health Equity
abstract: There are concerns about the fairness of clinical prediction models. “Fair” models are defined as those for which their performance or predictions are not inappropriately influenced by protected attributes such as ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic status. Researchers have raised concerns that current algorithmic fairness paradigms enforce strict egalitarianism in healthcare, leveling down the performance of models in higher-performing subgroups instead of improving it in lower-performing ones. We propose assessing the fairness of a prediction model by expanding the concept of net benefit, using it to quantify and compare the clinical impact of a model in different subgroups. We use this to explore how a model distributes benefits across a population, its impact on health inequalities, and its role in the achievement of health equity. We show how resource constraints might introduce necessary trade-offs between health equity and other objectives of healthcare systems. We showcase our proposed approach with the development of two clinical prediction models: (1) a prognostic type 2 diabetes model used by clinicians to enroll patients into a preventive care lifestyle intervention programme and (2) a lung cancer screening algorithm used to allocate diagnostic scans across the population. This approach helps modelers better understand if a model upholds health equity by considering its performance in a clinical and social context.
score_reason: Discussion of algorithmic fairness using net benefit; relevant to prediction methodology.

title: Considerations for the Analysis of Urinary Environmental Chemical Concentrations During Pregnancy
abstract: Background: Pregnancy physiology may impact indicators of hydration, affecting exposure assessment in gestational studies with urinary chemical biomarkers. Methods: We aimed to characterize hydration and demonstrate the impact of different methods for standardizing urinary chemical biomarker concentrations on exposure descriptives in the Human Placenta and Phthalates Study (n = 303, 2017–2020), a prospective pregnancy cohort with eight study visits between 12 and 38 weeks of gestation. We assessed trajectories and predictors of hydration using urine flow rate (UFR) and specific gravity (SG). Likewise, we examined trajectories and predictors of mono-n-butyl phthalate (MBP), for which concentrations were unstandardized or standardized via UFR (analyte excretion rates), SG alone (Boeniger method), or covariate-adjusted SG (O’Brien method). We used generalized additive mixed effects models to examine trajectories. We used linear mixed effects models to investigate participant demographic and pregnancy characteristics influencing UFR and SG, and agreement between unstandardized and standardized MBP concentrations. Results: As pregnancy progressed, SG declined linearly, whereas UFR varied in a nonlinear manner. Several demographic and pregnancy characteristics, notably race and ethnicity, were associated with UFR and SG. Unstandardized and standardized MBP concentrations showed good agreement, with lower agreement observed between concentrations standardized using UFR (analyte excretion rates) relative to SG (Boeniger and O’Brien methods). Nevertheless, trajectories and predictors of MBP concentrations were similar across all standardization approaches. Conclusions: Despite systematic variations in hydration across gestation and by demographic and pregnancy characteristics, methods commonly used for standardizing urinary concentrations of chemical biomarkers were robust to differences in the hydration indicator as well as the standardization method employed.
score_reason: Methodological considerations for urinary biomarkers in pregnancy; relevant to exposure assessment in epidemiology.

title: Development and Validation of Gestational Age Estimation Algorithms for Nonlive Births in Administrative Healthcare Databases
abstract: Background: Algorithms to estimate gestational age (GA) for nonlive births have been developed in other administrative healthcare databases, but their applicability in Korea remains unknown. We adapted algorithms developed in the United States and evaluated their validity in Korean healthcare claims data. Methods: Using the National Health Information Database of South Korea, we linked GA information on influenza vaccination from the national vaccination registry to establish a reference standard. Nonlive births were stratified into spontaneous/induced abortions and stillbirths. Four algorithms were tested: (1) assigning outcome-specific GA, (2) adjusting GA based on ultrasound scan records, (3) a regression model using gestational markers as predictors, and (4) a random forest model. Algorithms were evaluated by the proportion of estimates within 1–4 weeks of the reference standard and the mean squared error (MSE). External validation was conducted using an independent dataset. Results: Random forests performed best for both spontaneous/induced abortions (MSE 1.68 weeks 2 ) and stillbirths (MSE 0.97 weeks 2 ), with 92.6% (95% confidence interval 91.6, 93.4) and 97.4% (96.2, 98.3) of predictions falling within 2 weeks of the reference standard, respectively. However, in the external validation set, the ultrasound record-based adjustment approach performed similarly to the random forest approach for both spontaneous/induced abortions (MSE 8.37 vs. 8.15 weeks 2 ) and stillbirths (MSE 12.42 vs. 12.52 weeks 2 ). Conclusions: Deterministic approaches may be preferable for estimating GA of nonlive births in the National Health Information Database, as they are simpler to implement and perform comparably to model-based algorithms. These algorithms can support pregnancy research in the Korean population.
score_reason: Algorithm validation for gestational age estimation, good gateway reading for data quality methods.

title: A Framework for Thinking About the Potential Public Health Impact of Epidemiologic Research
abstract: An impactful epidemiologic question is one that, if answered, could inform meaningful action to reduce the burden of disease in the population it concerns. We propose a set of factors that could be used for discussing, evaluating, and communicating the public health impact of epidemiologic studies. These factors pertain to the burden and distribution of disease, the potential for an intervention to alter the disease burden, and the context in which the study is conducted. The disease burden is characterized by the number of cases, severity or cost of disease, and distribution of disease across the population. The potential for intervention is characterized by the mutability of the exposure itself, the prevalence and distribution of other causes of the disease in the population, the prevalence of the exposure and risk of the outcome under the natural course (before any intervention), and the feasibility of intervening. An epidemiologic question need not be impactful along all these factors to make answering it worthwhile. However, answering epidemiologic questions with more of these factors present will likely have a greater public health impact than answering questions for which these factors are absent. We hope that collecting these factors into a single framework may aid students and senior epidemiologists alike when organizing arguments for the value of their own work or attempting to evaluate the impact of others’ work.
score_reason: Conceptual framework; no statistical methodology.

title: Novel Psychometric Indicator Assessments: The Relative Excess Correlation and Associated Matrices
abstract: For a series of indicators used to assess psychosocial constructs, we propose reporting new types of correlation matrices to gain greater insight into the relation of the indicators with one another. What we define as the observed residual correlation (ORC) matrix can give insight as to whether, when a given indicator is above the indicator-average scores across all indicators for that individual, what other indicators might be anticipated to be above that individual’s average score as well. What we define as the relative excess correlation (REC) matrix can give insight, for each pair of indicators, whether the strength of that particular correlation is above or below what might have been anticipated based on the correlation of each of those two indicators with all of the others. The ORC and REC matrices will, generally, have numerous negative entries even if all of the raw correlations between each pair of indicators are positive. We discuss the properties of, and the relations between, these correlation matrices, and their analogues for covariances. The positive deviations of the REC matrix entries from zero also can help identify clusters of indicators that are more strongly related to one another, providing insights somewhat analogous to factor analysis, but without the need for decisions concerning rotations or the number of factors. However, the ORC and REC matrices can also be used purely descriptively to provide insights into understanding the relation of indicators with one another.
score_reason: Novel psychometric correlation matrices; limited overlap with primary interests.
key_techniques: no need for rotation or factor number decisions

title: Re: Confounders, Mediators, or Colliders: What Types of Shared Covariates Does a Sibling Comparison Design Control For?
abstract: To the Editor: I write regarding Sjölander and Zetterqvist’s1 methodological contribution on sibling comparison designs. While their framework helpfully distinguishes between confounders, mediators, and colliders, their claim that shared family environment may be a mediator does not clearly differentiate between biological mechanisms operating during pregnancy and social pathways operating through postnatal family circumstances. If a researcher’s scientific question concerns the biological impact of parental age, then family environment is a confounder, rather than a mediator, and conditioning on it in a sibling design would not remove but rather help isolate the portion of the effect of scientific interest. Mediators are variables that lie on the causal pathway from exposure to outcome. Sjölander and Zetterqvist write that in a prior sibling study of maternal age and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), attenuated within-family findings might reflect mediation through a shared family environment: that young maternal age leads to “financially difficult family situations” that increase ADHD risk.1,2 To classify shared family environment as a mediator, one must posit that parental age causally shapes the environment in which children are raised in a way that itself produces the outcome. But when the biological effects of age are under study—for example, through mechanisms related to gamete quality, placental function, or in-utero biological processes—we generally seek to isolate prenatal pathways that do not plausibly operate through the postnatal family environment. Family environment could potentially modify the magnitude of biological effects (i.e., if the biological impact of maternal age were larger or smaller depending on socioeconomic circumstances), but effect modification would not imply mediation, and would not change its status as a potential confounder, associated with both the exposure and outcome. If we were interested in the total biological and social effects of maternal age, family environment might constitute a mediator. But that alternative research question would examine maternal age as a social marker rather than a biological exposure. Put another way, for an expectant parent trying to understand biological effects—for example, the ADHD risk for their first child if they give birth at 40 compared to 30, all else equal—adjusting for family environment would remove confounding from socioeconomic factors, providing better estimates of the causal quantity of interest. Whether a variable acts as a confounder or mediator depends on the specific causal question. For biological hypotheses about maternal age effects (or other prenatal exposures, such as acetaminophen3), shared family environment confounds rather than mediates, making sibling comparison designs often well-suited for isolating biological effects.
score_reason: Brief commentary on sibling comparison designs, limited methodological depth.

title: Jørn Olsen, 20 May 1946–5 January 2026
abstract: We mourn the loss of Jørn Olsen, our friend, colleague, mentor, and reliable ethical compass. We are grateful for the great privilege of having worked with him. Jørn was the first professor of social medicine at Aarhus University (Denmark), where, with Johannes Ibsen, he built Denmark’s first epidemiology powerhouse. His earliest work was on occupational and perinatal epidemiology, and in the 1980s, he produced seminal papers on perinatal epidemiologic methods. In the 1990s, he led the Danish Epidemiology Science Centre. In 2006, he accepted a position as chair of the Department of Epidemiology at the University of California, Los Angeles, then returned to Aarhus University in 2011. Jørn was an extraordinarily productive scholar, with more than 650 peer-reviewed publications. His productivity was all the more remarkable because he was not a passive coauthor—he contributed substantial intellectual content to every paper he signed. His publications spanned epidemiologic methods, reproductive epidemiology, environmental epidemiology, social epidemiology, and virtually all forms of applied epidemiology—always with the goal of improving health. He revealed a more playful side in a series of insightful and entertaining articles in Danish. Jørn was a tireless advocate throughout his career for epidemiology, nationally and internationally. He defended free, unconventional academic thinking while championing truth and rigor. He sought to strengthen the contract between researchers and the public, emphasizing the importance of scientific integrity. He advocated for research on human health based on data from humans, saying tongue-in -cheek that “some humans may be rats, but rats are not humans.” He demonstrated his personal modesty in establishing a policy that data from his greatest achievement—the creation of the Danish National Birth Cohort—should be accessible to all researchers without requiring him to be a coauthor. He was deeply committed to international collaboration, serving as president of the International Epidemiological Association from 2005 to 2008 and organizing the European Congress of Epidemiology in Aarhus in 2013. He helped launch the European Educational Programme in Epidemiology, which has run a summer school in Florence since 1988. Jørn had a rich personal life as well, with a passion for sailing and devotion to his family—his wife, Ulla, three children, and six grandchildren. He will be sorely missed. Anne-Marie Nybo Andersen Cecilia Høst Ramlau-Hansen Allen J Wilcox
score_reason: Obituary, no research content.
